items.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: Maynard Ferguson Big Band with Wayne Shorter and Slide Hampton

ctx.x: How did your professors feel about that? Or wasn’t it even an issue for them?

Well most of them didn’t really care. I went to class on time and did the homework. Some of them didn’t care for that kind of music so they didn’t like what I did in classes, and the school did not encourage a jazz profile. And the strange thing is at that time there was the Eastman Theater, there was a show called “Jazz for Moderns” that would travel throughout the country. And they played at the Eastman Theater, it was a wonderful auditorium, it seated maybe 2,000 people. And they had great bands going all…
force in music, it’s hard to understand how a classical institution would continue to ignore its presence.

ctx.x: There’s something I didn’t know about Art Blakey. When I was doing...asked to do certain (over the years) interviews, I caught myself going back about Miles a lot, and Weather Report...Miles... But kind of recently, I caught myself. Wait a minute. I had five years with Art Blakey, and in those interviews I didn’t talk about it. But there was something about Art... Ok. I practice Buddhism. I’ll just leave it right there. But Herbie and I are...there’s a dialogue that we have had with a president of this Buddhist…

big German violin book, a method book for violin, and there was music paper in there of “Sentimental Over You” with the modern bebop changes written underneath, and a breakable record of Marcel Mule’s... [SINGS THE EXERCISE] She said to me, “I think he told me his name was Charlie Parker” [MIMICS FRENCH ACCENT, Char-lee Par-kehr...] It’s “Charl-lee Par-kehr...” Oh, no. She said, “It must have been Charlie Parker.” She’d worked with Art Blakey, just got in...a flood of history... She couldn’t have absorbed a whole…
